issues.issue: The Indemnifying Party's control of the defence is conditioned on a written acknowledgement "in form and substance satisfactory to the Claiming Party", a wholly subjective gate. Whether "promptly" notice is a condition of recovery is also unstated.
ENET covenants unqualified compliance with all laws, while the mirror covenant for the University in Section X.B.2 is qualified by "in all material respects".
"[R]easonable assurance of the funding necessary" states no amount, source or test, so the warranty cannot be measured against anything. The party is also mistyped as "EENET".
The University's compliance covenant is limited to "all material respects" whereas the mirror covenant in Section X.A.2 binds ENET without that qualifier.

The warranty that "Schedule B accurately identifies" the receive sites cannot be squared with Section III.B, which locates the receive sites on Schedule A, and with the several entries on Schedule B marked "Omitted".

The notification duty attaches to any event "which might reasonably be deemed to constitute a breach of or lead to a breach", a standard with no discernible threshold. What counts as an event that "might ... lead to" a breach is unbounded.

The cure conditions are joined by "either (a) ... or (b)", so on the literal text the University may terminate whenever a breach is uncured in thirty days even though ENET has undertaken substantive cure measures, which makes limb (b) meaningless. The parenthetical carve-out for money breaches sits inside limb (b) only.

The cure conditions are again joined disjunctively ("either is not cured ... or the University has not undertaken material or substantive measures"), so the second limb adds nothing and the two limbs give inconsistent results. "[M]aterial or substantive measures" is itself unmeasured.

Limb (3) lets ENET terminate on its own act of ceasing service, which is hard to reconcile with Section III.A, which withholds the University's equipment purchase option where ENET has exercised "its rights under Section XI.B.(2)".

Preserving the terminating party's damages claims is in tension with Sections XI.A and XI.B, which give each party a right to terminate "without further liability" to the other, and with Sections II.D and II.E, which terminate "without further liability between the parties".

The qualifier "subject to the approval of the University, which approval shall not be unreasonably withheld" is dropped into the middle of the sentence between the documents and the words "required to secure FCC approval", so what it modifies is unclear. The second sentence then makes University consent absolute, contradicting the reasonableness limit.

The absolute prohibition on any FCC filing without the University's advance consent cannot be squared with Section II.A.2, which requires the University to file the FCC Applications within thirty days or negotiate, and with Section II.B's duty to prosecute diligently.

The section uses "best reasonable efforts" in one sentence and "reasonable best efforts" in another, neither defined, alongside a flat duty to "fully cooperate with all reasonable requests". The differing formulations invite argument that different standards were intended.
This uncapped reimbursement duty must be read with Section XIII.N, which opens "[n]otwithstanding anything to the contrary" and caps legal and engineering fees at $15,000 for certain work.

The second sentence, "Subject to the foregoing provisions, the University may assign its authorization to an entity that does not agree to assume all remaining obligations", contradicts the first sentence, which permits assignment only if the assignee assumes those obligations. The words "[s]ubject to the foregoing provisions" cannot save a permission that is the opposite of what precedes it.

The same license-disposal machinery, including the ENET designation right and one year's notice, already appears in Section VIII.B, but there ENET's fee obligations are stated without the $15,000 cap set out here.

"ENET shall assist in the development of such program" states an obligation with no content, cost allocation or standard of performance. The program itself is described only as the University's "intention".

The integration clause states the entire agreement "with respect to the subject matter", yet Section XIII.Q subordinates the University's obligations to the separate Hybrid Agreement, which governs part of the same channel capacity.

The excuse extends to "other orders or requirements ... or other contingencies beyond the reasonable control of the parties" after a list of fires, strikes, embargoes and the like, leaving the catch-all's reach against the enumerated specifics open. The closing phrase "the period of dependency of any such contingency" is garbled.
The automatic extension of all time requirements sits against Section XIII.R, which makes every time for performance of the essence.

The covenant not to "take any action which would adversely affect the rights granted by it to the other party" is unlimited and could be read to override specific rights conferred elsewhere. "[B]est efforts" to execute further documents is likewise unmeasured.

The Agreement is made subject to the Communications Act, the FCC's Rules and District of Columbia law together, with no hierarchy if they diverge. Which body of law supplies the rules of construction is therefore open.

"District of Columbia courts" may mean the local D.C. courts only or any court sitting in the District, and "any party shall have the right to sue" may be permissive or exclusive. Both readings are available on the face of the clause.

Notices are deemed given on the first weekday after being sent by two named carriers only, with no rule for refusal or for notices sent by other means. The opening carve-out "[e]xcept as set forth above concerning the payment of Royalties" is not tied to a numbered section.

ENET is given an "exclusive right to lease the capacity of channel D2 for the duration of this Agreement" but must exercise it within twenty-one days of a notice, so it is unclear whether the right survives non-exercise. The additional royalty formula omits any statement that the ten cents is per month.
The option over channel D2 is difficult to reconcile with Section XIII.Q, which subordinates all of ENET's rights to Hybrid's rights in channel D2 under the Hybrid Agreement.

The $15,000 cap on negotiation legal and engineering fees conflicts with Section II.F, which puts "[a]ll reasonable costs and expenses, including legal and engineering, in connection with the preparation of this Agreement" on ENET without limit.

The trigger is a regulatory change that "would adversely affect the ability of the parties to perform", with no threshold, and the remedy is only a duty to "negotiate in good faith" — an agreement to agree. Nothing states what happens if negotiations fail.
This paragraph cites the FCC's Report and Order in MM Docket No. 93-106 as released July 9, 1994, whereas Section IV cites the same Report and Order (FCC 94-147) as released July 6, 1994.

The proviso that "no action shall be taken hereunder" if in the University's reasonable judgment it would adversely affect Hybrid gives the University a unilateral escape from any obligation, which is hard to reconcile with the Section IV capacity grant and the Section XIII.M option over channel D2.

Making every stated time of the essence pulls against Section XIII.F, which automatically extends all notice and performance periods for force majeure, and against the several "best efforts" and "as soon as reasonably possible" duties.

The clause preserves rights after an "express or implied waiver", but does not say what an implied waiver is or whether the waived breach itself remains actionable. Its reference to failures "in the future or in the past" is also confused.

The Final Order definition drives the termination triggers in Sections II.D, II.E and III.A, but Section II.E.3 sets a ten-day window running from "such event" without saying that finality is required there.
